periods.activity_title: What Is a Market? Mapping Needs, Wants, and Names

time_bands.activity: The teacher writes three columns on the board: 'Things I must have to survive,' 'Things I want but could live without,' and 'Places where I get them.' Students individually list three items in each column in their notebooks. The teacher takes three or four responses aloud and marks them under 'needs' or 'wants,' keeping the terms open for now.

The teacher introduces the term 'market' as the mechanism through which goods and services reach people, and explains that it carries different names in different regions — bazaar, haat, mārukatté — and can be a physical location or online. Students are asked: 'Which of your listed items can be bought in a market near your home? Which require you to go further, or to go online?' Partners discuss and report back.

The teacher reads aloud the description of Hampi Bazaar: Portuguese traveller Domingos Paes called Hampi 'the best-provided city in the world,' noting grains, silk, animals, and precious stones; Fernao Nuniz described craftsmen working golden jewellery, rubies, diamonds, and pearls in the streets. Students answer in writing: 'What does this description tell you about what a prosperous market looks like? Which items here are needs and which are wants?'

Class shares responses. The teacher closes by connecting the two threads: markets satisfy both needs and wants, connect communities, and have done so across history — the Hampi Bazaar shows this was true centuries ago just as it is true of markets today.

periods.section_context: Hampi Bazaar, Paes and Nuniz accounts, needs vs wants
periods.teacher_notes: Open with the two-column individual task before introducing any vocabulary so students commit to their own understanding first. A common confusion is that 'needs' and 'wants' are entirely personal — nudge students to see that needs are defined by survival, not by preference. The Hampi excerpts anchor an abstract definition in a vivid historical case.

competency_edges.competency_text: Understanding trade, commerce, and markets as mechanisms through which commodity production, trade, and commerce reach consumers.
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can distinguish between needs and wants and explain how markets function as the mechanism connecting producers and consumers.

competency_edges.competency_text: Recognising evidence of India's historically prosperous markets and civilisational wisdom.
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can interpret traveller accounts as evidence of a market's historical prosperity and range of traded goods.

periods.activity_title: How Prices Are Decided: The Guava Negotiation
materials: Role-card strips (buyer/seller — prepared by teacher on paper)

time_bands.activity: The teacher draws three boxes on the board labelled 'Price too high,' 'Price too low,' and 'Price just right,' each containing a stick figure of a buyer and a seller. Students are asked: 'In the guava scenario: if the seller asks ₹100 for a dozen guavas, what happens? If the seller asks ₹2?' Students call out responses while the teacher annotates the boxes — seller happy/buyer refuses; buyer happy/seller loses money.

Pairs receive role-card strips: one card says 'You are the guava seller — you paid ₹15 for the guavas and need to make a profit' and the other says 'You are the buyer — you have ₹25 and want at least a dozen guavas.' Pairs negotiate aloud and record the price they agreed on (or note if they could not agree). The teacher polls three or four pairs and writes their agreed prices on the board.

The teacher asks: 'Why did different pairs land on different prices? What would happen if fifty sellers all had guavas and only five buyers wanted them? What if fifty buyers wanted guavas and only five sellers had them?' Students discuss in their pairs and then write two sentences answering: 'How do the quantity offered by sellers and the quantity demanded by buyers together shape the price that emerges?'

The teacher draws a simple T-chart: 'What the seller needs from a price' vs 'What the buyer needs from a price.' Students contribute entries and the teacher frames the definition: price is the amount at which a willing buyer and a willing seller agree, shaped by their repeated interactions. Students copy the definition with one example of their own.

periods.section_context: Guava price scenarios, buyer-seller negotiation, price determination
periods.teacher_notes: Having introduced what markets are and the goods they carry, this unit moves to the mechanism inside every transaction — price. Students often assume sellers always set prices unilaterally; the simulation surfaces the mutual dependency. Watch for pairs who simply split the difference without reasoning — press them: 'What constraint did your seller card give you?'

competency_edges.competency_text: Understanding trade, commerce, and markets as mechanisms through which commodity production, trade, and commerce reach consumers.
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can explain how buyer willingness, seller cost, and relative quantities together determine a market price.

periods.activity_title: Physical vs Online Markets: Comparing Where We Buy
periods.section_anchor: Markets Around Us — Physical and Online Markets
materials: Printed or hand-drawn comparison chart template (one per student)
periods.visual_aids: Two-column comparison chart: 'Physical Market' | 'Online Market' with rows for Location, How buyer finds goods, How payment works, Delivery, Advantages, Disadvantages

time_bands.activity: The teacher distributes the comparison chart template. Students individually fill in what they already know or have experienced about physical markets (weekly haats, local bazaars, malls) and online markets (shopping apps, websites) before any instruction — this activates prior knowledge and shows the teacher where gaps exist.

The teacher builds the chart on the board using student responses as a starting point, adding what the chapter supplies: physical markets require in-person meeting and immediate payment; online markets allow buyers and sellers to transact from any location, offer home delivery, and allow manufacturers to procure inputs — for example, a factory ordering raw materials through a portal. The teacher asks: 'Can you buy an online class? How is a service different from a good in this context?'

Students write three analysis questions in their notebooks and answer them: (1) 'Which market type gives the buyer more choice — and why?' (2) 'What problems might a buyer face in an online market that they would not face in a physical one?' (3) 'A small farmer in a village wants to sell her vegetables to buyers in a city 400 km away — which market type helps her more, and what does she need to use it?' Students share answers in pairs.

The teacher takes whole-class responses to question 3 — the farmer scenario — to close the unit by showing that market type is not merely a matter of convenience but affects who can participate in trade and how. Students complete their comparison chart with any corrections or additions.

periods.section_context: Physical haats, malls, online apps, home delivery, manufacturer procurement
periods.teacher_notes: A common confusion is that 'online market' means only consumer shopping; the unit extends this to manufacturer input procurement and service delivery, as the chapter does. Students who have limited personal online shopping experience can still engage through the farmer scenario, which shifts from personal experience to structural analysis. The completed chart is a reference tool for this unit's work.

competency_edges.competency_text: Understanding trade, commerce, and markets as mechanisms through which commodity production, trade, and commerce reach consumers.
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can compare physical and online market types by analysing how each enables or constrains participation by buyers, sellers, and manufacturers.

periods.activity_title: Domestic and International Markets: India's Trade Flows
periods.section_anchor: Markets Around Us — Domestic and International Markets
materials: Blank outline map of the world (one per student or pair)
periods.visual_aids: Outline world map with India, West Asia, Africa, North America, Europe, and South East Asia labelled

time_bands.activity: The teacher distributes blank outline maps. Students are asked: 'If you wanted to buy crude petroleum, where might India get it from? If India sells software, who might buy it?' Students mark their guesses with arrows on the map — exports out of India, imports into India — before seeing the chapter's data.

The teacher introduces domestic markets — where goods and services are bought and sold within a country's boundaries, like paper from Indian paper mills for Indian textbooks — and international markets, where sellers export and buyers import across borders. The teacher then displays the chapter's trade data: India exports software to North America, pharmaceuticals to Africa, and engineering goods to Europe; India imports crude petroleum from West Asia, diamonds from Africa, and vegetable oils from South East Asia. Students correct or confirm their map arrows and label each trade flow.

Students answer in writing: (1) 'What does India's export of pharmaceuticals to Africa tell you about what India produces and what Africa needs?' (2) 'Why might India import diamonds from Africa rather than buy them from within India?' (3) 'Choose one import and explain what would happen to Indian consumers if that import were suddenly stopped.' Students compare answers with a neighbour.

The teacher draws out the key principle: international markets exist because no country produces everything its people need — trade across borders distributes resources across geographies. Students add a two-sentence summary to their maps before the close.

periods.section_context: India's exports to North America, Africa, Europe; imports from West Asia, South East Asia
periods.teacher_notes: Having worked on how prices form in any market, students now encounter the geographic scale at which markets operate — from domestic to international. A common confusion is treating imports as a sign of weakness; the writing questions redirect students toward interdependence as the operative concept. The map annotation gives a spatial anchor to what is otherwise an abstract set of trade flows.

competency_edges.competency_text: Understanding trade, commerce, and markets as mechanisms through which commodity production, trade, and commerce reach consumers.
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can trace how goods move between domestic and international markets and explain why countries engage in cross-border trade.

competency_edges.competency_text: Understanding how resources are distributed across geographies through international trade.
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can map the geographic distribution of traded resources and explain why international trade reflects uneven resource availability across countries.

periods.activity_title: Wholesalers, Retailers, and Distributors: Who Does What?
materials: Strips of paper for flow-chart activity (one set per group of four)

time_bands.activity: The teacher poses the question: 'A rice farmer in Punjab grows 10,000 kg of rice. How does it reach the kitchen of a family in Chennai?' Students brainstorm in groups of four and write the steps they imagine on strips of paper, one step per strip, without any instruction.

The teacher introduces the chapter's supply chain: producers/farmers → wholesalers (who buy in large quantities, store in godowns, use cold storage for perishables, and bring produce to mandīs) → distributors (who bridge the gap when wholesalers cannot reach many retailers due to distance and terrain) → retailers (shopkeepers who sell in small quantities to final consumers for personal use, not resale). Examples include Khari Baoli spice market in Old Delhi and Asia's oldest textile market in Surat. Groups rearrange their strips to match this chain and add any missing actors.

Groups receive three analysis questions on the board: (1) 'Why does a wholesaler need a godown, while a retailer usually does not?' (2) 'When would a distributor be needed between the wholesaler and the retailer? Give a real-world example.' (3) 'What would happen to the price of rice if all distributors in a hilly region disappeared overnight?' Groups discuss and write two-sentence answers to each.

Groups present their answer to question 3 aloud. The teacher closes by showing how each actor in the chain adds a function — storage, transport, breaking bulk — and that removing any link changes the price or availability of goods for consumers.

periods.section_context: Wholesalers, godowns, mandīs, Khari Baoli, Surat textile market, distributors, retailers
periods.teacher_notes: The chapter distinguishes three roles — wholesaler, distributor, retailer — that students frequently collapse into 'middleman.' The strip-sequencing task forces students to commit to an order before the teaching, making the correction more memorable. Cold storage and mandīs are key vocabulary to reinforce, as they appear in the Surat supply-chain illustration later in the chapter.

competency_edges.competency_text: Understanding trade, commerce, and markets as mechanisms through which commodity production, trade, and commerce reach consumers.
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can trace the roles of wholesalers, distributors, and retailers in moving goods from producers to consumers and analyse what each role contributes.

periods.activity_title: The Surat Textile Supply Chain: Cotton to Consumer
materials: Printed Surat supply-chain diagram or teacher-drawn version on chart paper
periods.visual_aids: Flow diagram: Raw cotton (nearby states) → Weaving → Dyeing → Finishing → Wholesale market → Small shopkeepers / Large retail stores → Consumers (India and international)

time_bands.activity: The teacher displays the Surat supply-chain diagram. Students read it silently and write three observations: one thing that surprised them, one question the diagram raises, and one connection to something they already know about markets.

The teacher walks through the diagram step by step: raw cotton arrives from nearby states; it passes through weaving, dyeing, and finishing — three distinct production stages — before entering the wholesale market. From there, goods flow to small shopkeepers and large retail stores across India, and then internationally. The teacher asks at each stage: 'What value is being added here? Who is paying for that added value, and who ultimately bears the cost?'

Students write a structured analysis in their notebooks with three sections: (a) 'List every actor in the Surat supply chain from cotton grower to final consumer.' (b) 'At which stage does the product change form, and at which stages does it only change hands?' (c) 'If the price of raw cotton doubles, trace how that cost might move through the chain to the person buying a sari in a shop in Chennai.'

The teacher takes whole-class responses to section (c) of the analysis — the cost-tracing task — and draws the chain on the board, annotating where price increases are absorbed or passed on. The close affirms: a physical supply chain is a sequence of value-adding and cost-accumulating steps, and every step shapes what the consumer pays.

periods.section_context: Surat textile chain, raw cotton, weaving, dyeing, finishing, wholesale, retail flow
periods.teacher_notes: Building on the roles of wholesalers and retailers established in the previous unit's framework, this unit zooms in on one complete, documented supply chain. The cost-tracing task in section (c) is the highest-demand move — students must reason causally through each stage rather than merely list actors. If students struggle, ask them to focus on just two consecutive stages first.

competency_edges.competency_text: Understanding trade, commerce, and markets as mechanisms through which commodity production, trade, and commerce reach consumers.
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can trace how production stages and distribution actors accumulate cost and value along a commodity's supply chain from raw material to consumer.

periods.activity_title: Online Aggregators: How the Digital Supply Chain Works
periods.visual_aids: Flowchart: Manufacturer (bulk) → Aggregator warehouse → Aggregator app/website → Online buyer (home delivery)

time_bands.activity: The teacher puts the online distribution flowchart on the board and asks: 'Where is the wholesaler in this chain? Where is the retailer? Or are they the same actor wearing a different name?' Students write their initial answers individually before discussion begins.

The teacher explains the aggregator model: manufacturers send bulk quantities to an aggregator's warehouse; the aggregator runs a website or mobile application that organises and combines offers from multiple sellers; the aggregator packs and delivers directly to the online buyer. Students compare this with the physical chain (from units 5 and 6) by writing a two-column table: 'Physical chain actor' vs 'Online chain equivalent,' identifying what the aggregator combines from the physical chain.

The teacher poses three evaluative questions for written response: (1) 'Does the aggregator model reduce or increase the number of steps from producer to consumer? Explain your reasoning.' (2) 'Who benefits most from the aggregator model — the manufacturer, the consumer, or small shopkeepers? Support your answer.' (3) 'Name one type of product that would work well in an aggregator model and one that would not, and explain why.'

Students share answers to question 2 aloud. The teacher closes by noting that the digital supply chain is not shorter in terms of labour — it reorganises who holds stock and who delivers it, shifting warehousing from many small retailers to a single centralised aggregator.

periods.section_context: Aggregator model, bulk to warehouse, website-organised sellers, home delivery
periods.teacher_notes: Having mapped the physical Surat supply chain, students can now contrast it with the digital aggregator model — the comparison sharpens both. A common confusion is that 'aggregator' simply means 'online shop'; stress that the distinctive function is combining multiple sellers onto one platform and centralising packing and delivery. The evaluative question on winners and losers prompts normative thinking grounded in the chapter's content.

competency_edges.competency_text: Understanding trade, commerce, and markets as mechanisms through which commodity production, trade, and commerce reach consumers.
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can evaluate how the aggregator model reorganises the supply chain and assess its effects on different market participants.

periods.activity_title: What Markets Do for People: Economic and Social Roles
periods.section_anchor: The Role of Markets in People's Lives

time_bands.activity: The teacher writes two headings on the board: 'Economic role of markets' and 'Non-economic role of markets.' Students are asked: 'We have been studying markets as mechanisms for buying and selling — but do markets do anything beyond that? Write two ideas under each heading before we discuss.' Students write individually.

The teacher builds on student responses. Economic roles: markets facilitate transactions between producers and consumers; they signal to producers what consumers want — the example of energy-efficient refrigerators shows how consumer demand drives production decisions, benefiting society through better products. Non-economic roles: long-lasting trusted relationships between buyers and sellers, sometimes continuing across generations; markets as social spaces where communities exchange ideas and traditions.

Students read the Ima Keithal description from the board (teacher writes key facts): approximately 3,000 women own and run all shops in Imphal, Manipur; goods include vegetables, traditional Manipuri attire, handloom and handicrafts, daily essentials; the market provides employment and income for thousands of families and serves as a meeting point for different communities. Students answer: (1) 'Identify one economic role and one non-economic role that Ima Keithal performs.' (2) 'What makes this market unusual compared to others you have studied?' (3) 'The haldi-kumkum practice in south India — is it an economic act, a social act, or both? Explain.'

The class discusses the haldi-kumkum question — the teacher uses it to show that the boundary between economic and non-economic functions is porous, and that markets carry cultural meanings alongside commercial ones. Students add a one-sentence synthesis to their notebooks: 'Markets do more than move goods because…'

periods.section_context: Ima Keithal Imphal, energy-efficient refrigerator signal, haldi-kumkum tradition, generational trust
periods.teacher_notes: Having studied how goods move through supply chains, students now examine why markets matter beyond logistics. The Ima Keithal example is powerful for gender equity discussions — resist the temptation to frame it only as a curiosity; press students to identify its structural economic role first. The haldi-kumkum example is deliberately ambiguous, which is its pedagogical value.

competency_edges.competency_text: Understanding trade, commerce, and markets as mechanisms through which commodity production, trade, and commerce reach consumers.
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can analyse how markets function simultaneously as economic mechanisms and social spaces, drawing on concrete examples.

periods.activity_title: Price Controls: Protecting Buyers and Sellers Through Government Action
periods.section_anchor: Government's Role in the Market — Controlling Prices for Protecting Buyers and Sellers
materials: Case-card strips (two scenarios — one for each pair)

time_bands.activity: The teacher distributes two case-card strips. Strip A: 'A pharmaceutical company has developed a lifesaving antibiotic. They want to sell it at ₹2,000 per course of treatment. Many patients who need it cannot afford this price.' Strip B: 'Wheat farmers in Punjab spent ₹1,200 per quintal growing their crop, but grain merchants are offering them only ₹900 per quintal, which means farmers lose money.' Half the class receives Strip A and half receives Strip B. Each student writes: 'What problem does this situation create, and who is harmed?'

The teacher introduces the government's price control tools: maximum prices — the government sets an upper limit, as with lifesaving drugs, so buyers are protected; minimum prices — the Minimum Support Price for wheat, paddy, and maize ensures farmers do not incur losses; minimum wages ensure fair payment to employees. The teacher returns to each strip and asks: 'Which tool applies here? How does it address the harm you identified?'

Students work through a structured written task: 'For each of the three price control tools (maximum price, minimum price/MSP, minimum wage), write: (a) who it protects and from what harm, (b) a risk that arises if the controlled price is set too low or too high, and (c) one example from the chapter.' Students work individually and compare with a partner.

The teacher closes with the chapter's key tension: price controls protect one party but can create problems for the other — prices set too low remove producers' motivation, prices set too high disadvantage consumers. Students write one sentence capturing this trade-off in their own words.

periods.section_context: Lifesaving drug price cap, Minimum Support Price for wheat paddy maize, minimum wages
periods.teacher_notes: This unit opens the government regulation section of the chapter. Students often see government price controls as straightforwardly protective; the closing tension — that every control has a risk — complicates that intuition productively. The Kauṭilya reference appears in the Providing Public Goods subsection later; do not introduce it here.

competency_edges.competency_text: Understanding how the government as a political institution regulates markets through price controls, quality standards, pollution regulation, and public goods provision.
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can explain how maximum prices, minimum support prices, and minimum wages each protect a different market participant and analyse the risk of miscalibrating each tool.

competency_edges.competency_text: Understanding how government regulation directly shapes the economic conditions of buyers, sellers, and communities.
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can identify which social group each price control mechanism protects and explain how institutional decisions alter economic outcomes for buyers and sellers.

periods.activity_title: Quality and Safety: Standards, Certification, and Consumer Protection
periods.section_anchor: Government's Role in the Market — Ensuring Quality and Safety Standards
materials: Empty or printed product labels (teacher-sourced: food packet, electrical appliance, medicine box)
periods.visual_aids: Sample product label showing: FSSAI number, ISI mark, net quantity, MRP, batch number, best-before date, ingredients, allergen declaration

time_bands.activity: The teacher places (or draws on the board) a product label and asks: 'What information can you read on this label? Mark everything you recognise.' Students annotate individually. The teacher takes four or five responses and lists them on the board.

The teacher introduces the chapter's consumer quality tools in two layers. Layer 1 — label information: net quantity, date of manufacture, batch number, best-before date, MRP, name and address of manufacturer, nutrition facts, ingredients list, allergen declaration. Layer 2 — government certification marks: FSSAI (food safety), ISI/BIS (electrical appliances, construction materials, automotive tyres), AGMARK (agricultural products — vegetables, fruits, cereals, pulses, spices, honey), BEE Star Rating (electronic appliances; higher stars = greater energy efficiency = lower electricity bills). The teacher maps each mark to the product type it governs, using the label visual.

Students complete a classification task in their notebooks: 'For each product below, identify which certification mark you would look for and what it guarantees — (1) a bag of turmeric powder, (2) a ceiling fan, (3) a carton of honey, (4) a new air conditioner, (5) a packet of tablets from a pharmacy.' Students then write: 'Why does the government require manufacturers to obtain these marks rather than leaving it to buyers to judge quality for themselves?'

The class shares answers to the 'why' question. The teacher closes by connecting government quality certification to the price-control work of the previous unit — both are forms of market regulation that protect consumers when they cannot independently verify what they are buying.

periods.section_context: FSSAI, ISI/BIS, AGMARK, BEE Star Rating, product label components, pharmaceutical sample testing
periods.teacher_notes: Building on the price-control regulatory tools studied earlier, this unit extends the government's role to product quality. A common confusion is conflating ISI and FSSAI — be explicit: ISI covers manufactured goods (electrical, construction, automotive), FSSAI covers food. The classification task forces students to apply the distinction rather than just list the marks.

competency_edges.competency_text: Understanding how the government as a political institution regulates markets through price controls, quality standards, pollution regulation, and public goods provision.
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can classify government certification marks by product category and explain how mandatory quality standards protect consumers who cannot verify product safety independently.

periods.activity_title: External Costs and Public Goods: When Markets Fail Society
periods.section_anchor: Government's Role in the Market — Mitigating the External Effects of Markets

time_bands.activity: The teacher poses the scenario: 'A factory produces single-use plastic bags and sells them profitably. Families who never bought a plastic bag find their river clogged with them, and children in the area develop respiratory problems. Who pays for the harm?' Students write a two-sentence response before discussion.

The teacher introduces the concept of external effects: markets sometimes impose costs on people who are not party to the transaction. Factory pollution from goods like single-use plastics pollutes the environment and creates health risks for communities who did not choose to participate in that market. The government intervenes through strict regulations — bans, production limits, environmental standards — to prevent these costs from being borne by society at large.

The teacher introduces public goods: services like public parks, roads, and policing that are accessible to all members of society and whose present use does not diminish their availability for future use. Because no private producer can charge individuals for using a public road or a park effectively, the government provides these goods. The chapter's Kauṭilya reference is introduced here: the Arthaśhāstra instructed traders of clarified butter to give buyers a small additional measure to compensate for ghee sticking to the measuring can — showing consumer protection is an ancient principle. Students write: 'Explain in your own words why a private company would not build a public road, using the concept of public goods.'

Students share their public-goods explanations, and the teacher closes by connecting both halves: external effects and public goods are two different reasons why the market, left alone, does not serve all members of society — and both create a justification for government intervention that is as old as Kauṭilya.

periods.section_context: Single-use plastics pollution, public parks roads policing, Kauṭilya Arthaśhāstra ghee measure
periods.teacher_notes: Having examined price controls and quality certification as targeted interventions, this unit addresses two structural reasons markets need government oversight. Students often find 'external effects' abstract; the single-use plastics scenario, drawn directly from the chapter, grounds it in a familiar context. The Kauṭilya reference can feel like a digression — frame it as evidence that these are not new problems but ancient ones.

competency_edges.competency_text: Understanding how the government as a political institution regulates markets through price controls, quality standards, pollution regulation, and public goods provision.
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can explain why market failures — external costs and public goods — require government intervention and evaluate the government's regulatory role using historical and contemporary evidence.

competency_edges.competency_text: Understanding how government regulation directly shapes the economic conditions of buyers, sellers, and communities.
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can identify how market failures — pollution and the absence of public goods — impose costs on communities and explain how government intervention redistributes those costs.

competency_edges.competency_text: Recognising evidence of India's historically prosperous markets and civilisational wisdom.
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can cite Kauṭilya's Arthaśhāstra as textual evidence that consumer protection principles are rooted in India's civilisational tradition.

periods.activity_title: Reading Product Labels: Consumer Skills in Practice
periods.section_anchor: How Can Consumers Assess the Quality of Products and Services?
materials: Printed product label sheets (two different product labels per student — food and electrical)
periods.visual_aids: Two annotated label templates: one food product label (FSSAI, batch number, best-before, ingredients, allergens) and one electrical appliance label (ISI mark, BEE star rating, MRP, manufacturer address)

time_bands.activity: Students receive two printed label sheets. Without instruction, they annotate both: circle every piece of information they think is important for a buyer, underline anything they do not recognise, and put a question mark beside anything that might indicate risk or safety concern. This gives the teacher a quick reading of what students already know how to look for.

The teacher works through each label element systematically, connecting to the chapter: net quantity (are you getting what you paid for?), date of manufacture and batch number (traceability), best-before date (safety), MRP (price ceiling — connected to the government's maximum price controls from the earlier unit), name and address of manufacturer (accountability), nutrition facts and ingredients (health decisions), allergen declaration (safety for specific consumers). For the electrical label, the BEE star rating is explained: higher stars mean greater energy efficiency, lower electricity bills, and reduced environmental load.

Students complete a structured label-reading task: 'Using the food label provided, answer — (1) Is this product safe to eat today? How do you know? (2) Who manufactured it and how would you contact them if the product harmed you? (3) Should a person with a nut allergy buy this product? What tells you? (4) Which certification mark appears, and what does it guarantee?' Then for the electrical label: '(5) How many BEE stars does this appliance have, and what does that mean for your electricity bill?'

The teacher closes by returning to the chapter's framing question: 'How can consumers assess the quality of products?' Students write a three-item checklist — three things they will now look for on any product label — in their own words, as a practical take-away from this unit.

periods.section_context: Product label components, FSSAI, ISI, BEE star rating, MRP, allergen, best-before date
periods.teacher_notes: Having studied certification marks in the previous unit at a conceptual level, students now apply that knowledge to actual label reading — a performance task. If printed labels are unavailable, the teacher can draw a simplified label on the board with all required fields. A common gap: students know MRP as a price tag but do not connect it to the government's maximum price function — make that link explicit.

competency_edges.competency_text: Understanding trade, commerce, and markets as mechanisms through which commodity production, trade, and commerce reach consumers.
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can apply product label information and certification marks to evaluate the quality, safety, and regulatory compliance of consumer goods.

periods.activity_title: Beyond Official Marks: Word-of-Mouth and Online Reviews
periods.section_anchor: How Can Consumers Assess the Quality of Products and Services?

time_bands.activity: The teacher asks: 'Think of the last time someone in your family bought something after being recommended by a neighbour or friend. What made that recommendation trustworthy? Write two reasons.' Students write individually.

The teacher introduces the two non-official consumer assessment tools from the chapter: word-of-mouth recommendations from family and friends (rooted in personal trust and shared experience), and online reviews and feedback from other consumers (available when shopping digitally, aggregating experience across many buyers). The teacher asks: 'What is the difference between a review from your grandmother and a review from a stranger online — in terms of trust, accuracy, and potential bias?'

Students work through a structured written comparison in three columns: 'Official certification marks,' 'Word-of-mouth recommendations,' 'Online reviews.' For each column they write: what it tells you, who produces it, what its limitations are, and when you would rely on it most. Students then answer: 'A friend wants to buy a second-hand air conditioner from an online seller who has no official certifications listed but has 200 five-star reviews. What advice would you give them, and why?'

Three or four students share their advice and reasoning. The teacher closes by noting that consumers typically use all three sources — official marks, trusted personal recommendations, and online reviews — in combination, and that none alone is sufficient. Students add this insight to their three-item checklist from the previous unit.

periods.section_context: Word-of-mouth family recommendations, online consumer reviews, digital shopping quality assessment
periods.teacher_notes: Having practised reading official labels and certification marks, students now examine the informal information channels that operate alongside them. The second-hand air conditioner scenario is designed to be genuinely evaluative — there is no single correct answer, only stronger and weaker reasoning. Students who rely exclusively on reviews without questioning their authenticity should be nudged toward the limitations column of their table.

competency_edges.competency_text: Understanding trade, commerce, and markets as mechanisms through which commodity production, trade, and commerce reach consumers.
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can evaluate the reliability of official certification marks, word-of-mouth recommendations, and online reviews as consumer quality-assessment tools and judge when each is most appropriate.

periods.activity_title: Market Simulation: Running a Classroom Market
materials: Product cards listing item name and quantity (teacher-prepared)

time_bands.activity: The teacher assigns roles: one-third of students are sellers (each with a product card naming their good and their production cost), two-thirds are buyers (each with a play-money slip showing their budget). The teacher announces: 'You have a fixed period to negotiate and transact. Record every attempted transaction — successful or not — and the price you agreed on or why you did not agree.'

The simulation runs: buyers move between sellers, negotiate prices, and complete transactions. The teacher observes without intervening, noting cases where no agreement is reached. After the simulation period, all students return to their seats and write: 'What price did you agree on (or why not)? What would have made you accept a lower price as a seller, or a higher price as a buyer?'

The teacher collects agreed prices from several seller-buyer pairs on the board, creating a visible spread. Students analyse: 'Why did different pairs transact at different prices for the same good? What happened when there were more buyers than sellers for a particular product? What happened when buyers had less money to spend?' Students write responses using the price-determination vocabulary established earlier: quantity demanded, quantity offered, negotiation, willingness to pay.

The teacher facilitates a closing discussion: 'In what ways did our classroom market resemble a real physical market? In what ways was it different?' Students identify at least two resemblances and two differences in their notebooks, connecting the simulation to the chapter's account of how price emerges from repeated buyer-seller interactions.

periods.section_context: Buyer-seller price negotiation, quantity demanded and offered, failed transactions
periods.teacher_notes: This simulation revisits price determination through full enactment, deepening the understanding first built in the guava negotiation unit. The observation task during the simulation — recording every transaction attempt — is critical; it generates the data for the analytical phase. Watch for students who avoid negotiating and just accept or reject the first offer — those cases are instructive for the analysis.

competency_edges.competency_text: Understanding trade, commerce, and markets as mechanisms through which commodity production, trade, and commerce reach consumers.
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can apply price-determination principles by participating in a simulated market and analysing how buyer and seller constraints produce observed transaction prices.

periods.activity_title: Government as Market Referee: Debating Four Regulatory Tools
periods.section_anchor: Government's Role in the Market — Controlling Prices for Protecting Buyers and Sellers
materials: Debate position cards (four positions — one per group)

time_bands.activity: The teacher divides the class into four groups and assigns each group a position card. Card 1: 'We represent wheat farmers — defend the Minimum Support Price.' Card 2: 'We represent patients who need lifesaving medicines — defend the maximum price cap on drugs.' Card 3: 'We represent pharmaceutical manufacturers — argue that the price cap reduces investment in new drugs.' Card 4: 'We represent consumers of packaged goods — argue that quality certification marks should be stronger.' Groups read their card and identify two arguments from the chapter that support their position.

Each group presents their position to the class in one to two minutes. After all four have presented, the teacher opens cross-examination: any group may ask a question of another group, which must respond using evidence from the chapter. The teacher facilitates without taking sides, ensuring all four positions receive at least one challenge.

Students individually write a structured response — not representing their group's assigned position but their own reasoning: 'Of the four government regulatory tools debated today — MSP, maximum drug price, pollution regulation, quality certification — which do you think is most important for protecting ordinary citizens, and why? Use at least two pieces of evidence from the chapter.'

The teacher closes by placing all four tools on the board and asking: 'Each tool protects a different person or community — which communities benefit from each?' Students call out answers, and the teacher annotates, showing that the government's regulatory role is not a single intervention but a multi-tool framework with different beneficiaries.

periods.section_context: MSP for farmers, drug price cap, pollution regulation, quality certification marks
periods.teacher_notes: This unit revisits the full landscape of government regulatory tools — price controls, quality standards, and pollution regulation — through a structured debate that forces students to reason from evidence rather than opinion. The closing individual writing task is the real assessment move; it separates assigned-position performance from genuine analysis. Ensure groups do not simply list facts but construct arguments.

competency_edges.competency_text: Understanding how the government as a political institution regulates markets through price controls, quality standards, pollution regulation, and public goods provision.
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can evaluate the relative effectiveness of different government market-regulation tools in protecting different social groups, using chapter evidence to support a reasoned position.

competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can argue from the perspective of a specific social group — farmers, patients, manufacturers, consumers — how a particular regulatory tool shapes their economic conditions.

periods.activity_title: Market Types: A Classification and Application Task
periods.section_anchor: Markets Around Us — Physical and Online Markets
materials: Scenario card set (one per pair — eight scenarios on a single printed or hand-written sheet)

time_bands.activity: The teacher distributes scenario cards listing eight market situations: (1) a farmer sells vegetables at a weekly haat, (2) a manufacturer orders industrial chemicals through a procurement portal, (3) a student buys a textbook from an online aggregator, (4) India exports pharmaceutical tablets to Nigeria, (5) a family buys spices from Khari Baoli, (6) a consumer subscribes to an online cooking class, (7) a textile wholesaler sells cloth to a retailer in Surat, (8) India imports crude petroleum from Saudi Arabia. Pairs read all eight silently.

Pairs classify each scenario into ALL applicable categories from the chapter's typology: physical / online; domestic / international; wholesale / retail. They must justify each classification in one phrase — for example, scenario 4 is 'online, international, wholesale.' The teacher circulates and flags disputed cases for whole-class discussion.

The teacher reviews two or three disputed classifications with the whole class, asking: 'Could a transaction be both domestic and wholesale? Could it be both online and retail? Which combinations are possible and which are not, and why?' Students then write a generalisation: 'The categories physical/online, domestic/international, and wholesale/retail are not mutually exclusive because…' and complete the sentence with an example.

Students create one new scenario of their own that fits at least three categories simultaneously, exchange with another pair, and classify each other's scenario. The teacher closes by noting that real markets are always intersections of multiple types — a single Surat transaction can be physical, domestic, and wholesale all at once.

periods.section_context: Physical, online, domestic, international, wholesale, retail market type combinations
periods.teacher_notes: Having studied each market type in its own unit, students now need to see that the categories are overlapping dimensions, not a mutually exclusive list. The classification task surfaces the most common error — treating the categories as a single hierarchy rather than three independent axes. The student-generated scenario at the close is a strong application check.

competency_edges.competency_text: Understanding trade, commerce, and markets as mechanisms through which commodity production, trade, and commerce reach consumers.
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can apply the chapter's market typology to classify real and hypothetical transactions across multiple dimensions simultaneously.

periods.activity_title: Reflective Essay: Markets, Regulation, and the Consumer I Am
periods.section_anchor: How Can Consumers Assess the Quality of Products and Services?

time_bands.activity: The teacher writes the essay prompt on the board: 'You are buying a new air conditioner for your home. Walk through every decision you would make — which market you would shop in, how you would assess quality and price, what government protections are in play, and what non-official sources you would consult — and explain your reasoning at each step.' Students read the prompt and spend two minutes listing the chapter concepts they will need to use.

Students write their reflective essays independently. The teacher circulates, prompting students who have stalled: 'Have you mentioned what type of market you are using? Have you checked a label or a certification mark? Have you thought about whether the price you see has any government involvement?' The essay should weave in: market type (physical or online), price assessment, BEE star rating, ISI mark if applicable, MRP, word-of-mouth or online reviews, and any government regulation that shapes the transaction.

Students exchange essays with a partner and annotate: circle every chapter concept correctly applied, underline any claim that needs more evidence, and write one question for the author. Authors read the annotation and add one paragraph responding to their partner's question.

The teacher closes by asking: 'Did your essay show that markets are just about buying and selling, or something more complex?' Two or three students read a sentence from their essay that captures the most complex insight they reached. The teacher affirms that the essay reflects the chapter's core argument: markets are layered systems shaped by price, regulation, certification, and social trust.

periods.section_context: Consumer air conditioner decision, BEE stars, ISI mark, MRP, online reviews, market type selection
periods.teacher_notes: Having covered the full range of consumer assessment tools — official labels, certification marks, and informal reviews — students now integrate these into a personal decision-making narrative. The peer annotation step is the quality-control mechanism; without it, essays tend to list concepts rather than apply them. Both drafting and peer review are completed inside this unit.

competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can construct a reasoned consumer decision-making account that integrates market type, price assessment, government regulation, and quality verification tools.

periods.activity_title: Chapter Synthesis: How Markets Work — From Hampi to Your Doorstep
materials: Large blank sheet of paper per group of four (for concept map)

time_bands.activity: Groups of four receive a large blank sheet. The teacher writes six anchor concepts on the board: 'Price determination,' 'Supply chain actors,' 'Market types,' 'Government's regulatory role,' 'Consumer quality assessment,' 'Markets as social spaces.' Each group places these six on their sheet and draws connecting lines — labelling each line with the relationship between the two concepts it joins. No further instruction is given; the task is to reconstruct the chapter's architecture from memory and reasoning.

Two groups share their maps, explaining the connections they drew — for example, 'We connected price determination to government's regulatory role because MSP and maximum prices are direct interventions in price.' The teacher probes: 'Where does Hampi Bazaar sit on your map? Where does Ima Keithal? Where does Kauṭilya?' Students add these historical and cultural anchors to their maps, showing that the chapter's argument runs from ancient markets to contemporary ones.

The teacher poses three synthesis questions for individual written response: (1) 'Adam Smith argued that prosperity emerges from markets that form when people need what they cannot produce themselves — which section of the chapter best supports this claim, and which complicates it?' (2) 'A factory in your town produces goods but pollutes the river. Using three tools from the chapter, explain what should happen.' (3) 'You are a wheat farmer in Punjab, a buyer of lifesaving medicine in Chennai, and a consumer buying an air conditioner online. In each role, name one market mechanism and one government action that shapes your situation.'

Students share responses to question 3 aloud. The teacher closes by writing on the board the chapter's opening quotation from Adam Smith and asking: 'After everything this chapter has shown us, is Smith's picture of markets complete — or does the chapter add something he left out?' Students write one final sentence in their notebooks. The teacher affirms: markets are ancient, adaptive, layered systems — facilitated and regulated by government, assessed by consumers, and embedded in social life.

periods.section_context: Price, supply chains, market types, government regulation, consumer tools, Hampi, Ima Keithal, Kauṭilya, Adam Smith
periods.teacher_notes: This synthesis unit is designed to work with whatever sections the class reached — the six anchor concepts span the chapter's full architecture, and students reconstruct connections rather than reproduce content. The Adam Smith question at the close is genuinely evaluative: the chapter affirms his insight while extending it to show that markets require regulation, trust, and institutional support. The concept map begins and ends inside this unit.

assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can distinguish between needs and wants and explain how markets function as the mechanism connecting producers and consumers.
assessment_items.question_text: A market is described in the chapter as the mechanism through which goods and services reach people. Which of the following best explains why markets satisfy both needs and wants?

options.label: A
options.text: Markets connect buyers and sellers for any good or service — essential or desired — enabling people to access what they cannot produce themselves.

options.label: B
options.text: Markets satisfy needs but not wants because sellers only produce what the government tells them to.

options.label: C
options.text: Markets satisfy wants first because sellers earn more profit from luxury goods than from essential goods.

options.label: D
options.text: Markets supply only essential goods like food, water, and shelter because sellers focus on what people must have.

what_each_option_reveals.D: Student confuses the chapter's definition of 'needs' with the full range of market goods — they have narrowed what markets supply to essentials only.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Student conflates government regulation of markets with control over what sellers may produce, misapplying the government's role section.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Student applies a profit-maximisation intuition that is not supported by the chapter's account — the chapter does not prioritise wants over needs in market operation.

competency.competency_text: Understanding trade, commerce, and markets as mechanisms through which commodity production, trade, and commerce reach consumers.

assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can trace how production stages and distribution actors accumulate cost and value along a commodity's supply chain from raw material to consumer.
assessment_items.question_text: In the Surat textile supply chain, raw cotton passes through weaving, dyeing, and finishing before reaching wholesale and retail markets. What best explains why the price a consumer pays for a finished textile is higher than the price the cotton grower received?

options.label: A
options.text: Each stage — weaving, dyeing, finishing, wholesale, retail — adds labour, skill, or service, and the cost of each addition accumulates in the final price.

options.label: B
options.text: Retailers in Surat charge high prices because they are the only sellers of textiles in India.

options.label: C
options.text: The government adds a tax at each stage of the Surat supply chain that raises the final price.

options.label: D
options.text: The price rises because raw cotton is scarce and cotton growers deliberately limit supply to raise their own income.

what_each_option_reveals.C: Student conflates value-addition with taxation — they recognise that each stage changes price but attribute it to government levies rather than accumulated production costs.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Student confuses market structure with market geography — the chapter's Surat example is an illustration, not a claim of monopoly.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Student applies a scarcity-of-raw-material reasoning from the price-determination section without connecting it to the supply chain's value-addition logic.

assessment_items.question_text: The chapter describes how online aggregators reorganise the supply chain by receiving bulk goods from manufacturers, combining offers from multiple sellers on a website or app, and delivering directly to buyers. A small shopkeeper who previously bought from a wholesaler and sold to local customers finds that buyers in the neighbourhood are now ordering the same goods online instead. Using the chapter's account of the aggregator model and the physical supply chain, evaluate who benefits and who is disadvantaged by the aggregator model.
look_for: Accurate description of the aggregator model: manufacturer sends bulk to aggregator warehouse; aggregator organises multiple sellers on an app or website; aggregator packs and delivers directly to buyer.
Identification of at least one beneficiary — e.g., online buyer (wider choice, home delivery) or manufacturer (direct bulk sales, reduced reliance on multiple wholesalers).
Identification of at least one disadvantaged party — e.g., small shopkeeper or local retailer who loses customers; traditional distributors whose bridging role is bypassed.
Evaluative reasoning: the student makes a judgement about net effect — not merely listing winners and losers but explaining the trade-off.
Optional credit: reference to the physical chain's actors (wholesaler, distributor, retailer) to contrast with the aggregator model.

assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can construct a connected account of how price determination, supply chain actors, market types, government regulation, and consumer assessment tools together constitute a functioning market system.
assessment_items.task: A new mobile phone has just been launched. It is manufactured in a factory, moves through a supply chain, is available in both physical stores and online, is sold in domestic and international markets, carries a government certification mark, and has 200 online customer reviews. Create a cause-effect map showing how each stage — production, distribution, market type, government regulation, and consumer quality assessment — connects to the next, and explain at each connection what would change if that stage were removed or disrupted.
assessment_items.scaffold: Start your map with the manufacturer at the top. Draw an arrow to the next actor in the supply chain and label what that actor does. Continue until you reach the final consumer. For each arrow, write one sentence: 'If [this stage] did not exist, then [this effect on the next stage or on the consumer].' Include government regulation and consumer quality assessment as nodes in your map — show where they connect into the chain.
format_of_output: A hand-drawn or written cause-effect map with labelled nodes and arrows
One sentence per arrow explaining the effect of removing that stage
Minimum six nodes: manufacturer, at least one supply chain actor, at least one market type, government regulation, consumer quality assessment, final consumer
assessment_items.inclusivity: Students who find drawing difficult may write a numbered sequence instead of a visual map, provided each step names the connection and the consequence of removing it. The teacher may pair students who need language support with a peer scribe.

OPEN_TASK.what_this_demonstrates: Students demonstrate the ability to construct a systemic account of how market components are interdependent — not merely listing stages but showing causal connections and evaluating the consequences of disruption at each node.
OPEN_TASK.reading_the_scaffold: The scaffold guides students to build the map sequentially from producer to consumer and to embed regulation and consumer tools as active nodes rather than afterthoughts. A student who lists all nodes but writes no causal sentences has completed the map but not the evaluation task.
OPEN_TASK.strong_vs_weak_markers: Strong responses: map includes all six required node types; causal sentences are specific (naming a real consequence, not generic harm); regulation and consumer assessment are connected to adjacent nodes with a clear mechanism; disruption consequences are distinct at each stage. Weak responses: map is a list of actors without arrows or causal labels; government regulation appears only as a label without a connection; disruption sentences repeat the same generic phrase ('everything would go wrong') across stages.
OPEN_TASK.format_rationale: The cause-effect map is the most natural demonstration vehicle for this LO because the chapter's core argument is systemic — price, supply chain, market type, regulation, and consumer tools are interdependent. A map with labelled causal arrows makes those interdependencies visible and evaluable in a way that a paragraph cannot.

competency.competency_text: Understanding how the government as a political institution regulates markets through price controls, quality standards, pollution regulation, and public goods provision.

assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can explain how maximum prices, minimum support prices, and minimum wages each protect a different market participant and analyse the risk of miscalibrating each tool.
assessment_items.chapter_section: Government's Role in the Market — Controlling Prices for Protecting Buyers and Sellers
assessment_items.question_text: The government sets a Minimum Support Price (MSP) for wheat. Which of the following best describes the risk the chapter identifies if the MSP is set too low?

options.label: A
options.text: Consumers will be unable to afford wheat because the price in shops rises above what families can pay.

options.label: B
options.text: Farmers will not be able to recover their production costs, removing their motivation to grow wheat.

options.label: C
options.text: The government will have to buy all the wheat itself because private buyers will refuse to purchase at a guaranteed price.

options.label: D
options.text: Wholesalers will store excess wheat in godowns and create an artificial shortage to drive up prices.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Student confuses the protective target of MSP — farmers — with the protective target of a maximum price cap, applying price-ceiling logic to a price-floor mechanism.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Student conflates the government's procurement role with the risk of miscalibration — a confusion between what the MSP mechanism does and what the chapter says happens when it is set too low.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Student imports supply-chain reasoning about wholesaler hoarding into a price-control question, conflating two distinct sections of the chapter.

competency.competency_text: Understanding how the government as a political institution regulates markets through price controls, quality standards, pollution regulation, and public goods provision.

assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can explain why market failures — external costs and public goods — require government intervention and evaluate the government's regulatory role using historical and contemporary evidence.
assessment_items.chapter_section: Government's Role in the Market — Mitigating the External Effects of Markets
assessment_items.question_text: A factory legally produces and sells single-use plastic bags. Families living near the factory find their river clogged with plastic waste, and children develop respiratory problems. The chapter says the government intervenes through strict regulations. Which statement best justifies this intervention?

options.label: A
options.text: The government intervenes because the factory has violated quality and safety certification standards required by ISI or FSSAI.

options.label: B
options.text: The government intervenes because the factory is not paying enough taxes on its plastic products.

options.label: C
options.text: The government intervenes because the factory is producing more than the market demands, causing prices to fall.

options.label: D
options.text: The government intervenes because the market transaction imposes costs — health and environmental harm — on people who did not participate in that transaction.

what_each_option_reveals.B: Student conflates government revenue concerns with the chapter's external-effects rationale — they recognise government involvement but misidentify the reason.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Student applies price-determination logic from the market mechanism section to a regulatory intervention question — conflating excess supply with external harm.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Student conflates the quality certification function of government regulation with the external-effects function — both involve government action, but for different reasons.

assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can classify government certification marks by product category and explain how mandatory quality standards protect consumers who cannot verify product safety independently.

competency.competency_text: Understanding how government regulation directly shapes the economic conditions of buyers, sellers, and communities.

assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can identify which social group each price control mechanism protects and explain how institutional decisions alter economic outcomes for buyers and sellers.
assessment_items.chapter_section: Government's Role in the Market — Controlling Prices for Protecting Buyers and Sellers
assessment_items.question_text: The government sets a maximum price on a lifesaving drug. Which of the following correctly identifies who is protected by this control and how it alters their economic situation?

options.label: A
options.text: Patients who need the drug are protected because the price cannot exceed the government's limit, keeping the drug within reach of more buyers.

options.label: B
options.text: Pharmaceutical manufacturers are protected because the maximum price guarantees them a minimum revenue for every unit sold.

options.label: C
options.text: The government itself is protected because it collects more tax revenue when prices are officially recorded and capped.

options.label: D
options.text: Wholesale distributors are protected because the price cap prevents retailers from undercutting them.

what_each_option_reveals.B: Student confuses maximum price with minimum price — applying the protective logic of MSP (seller protection) to a price-ceiling mechanism designed to protect buyers.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Student imports supply-chain actor reasoning into a price-control question, misidentifying who the regulatory tool targets.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Student conflates government regulation with government revenue, applying a taxation framework to a consumer-protection mechanism.

competency.competency_text: Understanding how government regulation directly shapes the economic conditions of buyers, sellers, and communities.

assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can identify how market failures — pollution and the absence of public goods — impose costs on communities and explain how government intervention redistributes those costs.
assessment_items.chapter_section: Government's Role in the Market — Mitigating the External Effects of Markets
assessment_items.question_text: The chapter explains that public goods like roads and public parks are provided by the government rather than private companies. Which of the following best explains why private companies would not provide public roads?

options.label: A
options.text: Private companies are not interested in roads because roads are always built in rural areas where profits are too low.

options.label: B
options.text: Private companies avoid roads because the government would immediately take over any road they build without paying compensation.

options.label: C
options.text: Private companies cannot effectively charge individual users of a public road, so they cannot recover their investment — the road generates no reliable profit.

options.label: D
options.text: Private companies cannot obtain the raw materials needed to build roads because the government controls all construction supplies.

what_each_option_reveals.D: Student applies a supply-side resource scarcity argument that has no basis in the chapter's account of public goods — they recognise government involvement but misidentify the mechanism.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Student imports a geographic profitability assumption irrelevant to the chapter's definition of public goods, confusing location-based reasoning with the non-excludability principle.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Student introduces a property-rights expropriation narrative that does not appear in the chapter — a fabricated distractor based on a misreading of government's role.

competency.competency_text: Understanding how resources are distributed across geographies through international trade.

assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can map the geographic distribution of traded resources and explain why international trade reflects uneven resource availability across countries.
assessment_items.chapter_section: Markets Around Us — Domestic and International Markets
assessment_items.question_text: The chapter states that India imports crude petroleum from West Asia and vegetable oils from South East Asia. What does this trade pattern most directly indicate about the geographic distribution of these resources?

options.label: A
options.text: Crude petroleum and certain vegetable oils are more abundantly available in specific regions of the world, and India sources them from those regions because they are not sufficiently available within its own boundaries.

options.label: B
options.text: India has a poor climate for agriculture and cannot produce any vegetable oils domestically.

options.label: C
options.text: India imports these goods because its government does not allow domestic production of petroleum and vegetable oils.

options.label: D
options.text: West Asia and South East Asia have lower wages than India, so it is always cheaper to import goods from those regions regardless of resource availability.

what_each_option_reveals.B: Student over-generalises from vegetable oil imports to a claim about India's entire agricultural capacity, misapplying the chapter's specific trade example.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Student substitutes a wage-based trade theory — not present in the chapter — for the chapter's resource-distribution explanation, importing an economic framework from outside the content.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Student attributes imports to a government prohibition that does not appear in the chapter, confusing trade regulation with resource availability.

competency.competency_text: Understanding how resources are distributed across geographies through international trade.

assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can map the geographic distribution of traded resources and explain why international trade reflects uneven resource availability across countries.
assessment_items.chapter_section: Markets Around Us — Domestic and International Markets
assessment_items.question_text: India exports software services to North America and pharmaceuticals to Africa. What does this pattern of exports reveal about India's position in international trade?

options.label: A
options.text: India exports goods and services in which it has productive capacity that other countries wish to access, while those countries supply India with what India lacks.

options.label: B
options.text: India exports only services and never goods, because Indian manufacturing is not competitive in international markets.

options.label: C
options.text: India exports these goods because the government requires all Indian manufacturers to sell at least half their output abroad.

options.label: D
options.text: India exports to North America and Africa because those are the only regions that are willing to trade with India.

what_each_option_reveals.B: Student incorrectly reads 'software and pharmaceuticals' as an exhaustive list, ignoring the chapter's mention of engineering goods exports and the domestic manufacturing sector.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Student applies a political exclusion narrative — 'only regions willing to trade' — that has no basis in the chapter, substituting geopolitical reasoning for resource-distribution logic.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Student invents a government export mandate that does not appear in the chapter, confusing trade regulation with the chapter's explanation of comparative resource availability.

competency.competency_text: Recognising evidence of India's historically prosperous markets and civilisational wisdom.

assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can interpret traveller accounts as evidence of a market's historical prosperity and range of traded goods.
assessment_items.question_text: Portuguese traveller Domingos Paes described Hampi as 'the best-provided city in the world,' while Fernao Nuniz described craftsmen working in the streets producing golden jewellery, rubies, diamonds, and pearls. What do these traveller accounts tell us about the Hampi Bazaar?

options.label: A
options.text: The accounts confirm that Hampi was the capital city of the Vijayanagara Empire and housed its royal court.

options.label: B
options.text: The accounts prove that Portuguese traders controlled the Hampi market and imported all the goods sold there.

options.label: C
options.text: The accounts serve as evidence of Hampi's commercial prosperity — a wide variety of goods was available and skilled craftsmen operated openly, indicating a thriving market.

options.label: D
options.text: The accounts show that Hampi was unusual because it sold luxury goods only to foreign visitors, not to local people.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Student conflates the Vijayanagara political context — which the chapter mentions briefly — with the chapter's purpose in citing Paes and Nuniz, which is commercial evidence, not political history.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Student misreads the travellers' role: Paes and Nuniz are observers and sources of evidence, not controllers or importers — a confusion between witness and actor.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Student introduces an exclusion narrative for foreign-only clientele that has no basis in the chapter's account, which emphasises the market's general abundance.

competency.competency_text: Recognising evidence of India's historically prosperous markets and civilisational wisdom.

assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can cite Kauṭilya's Arthaśhāstra as textual evidence that consumer protection principles are rooted in India's civilisational tradition.
assessment_items.chapter_section: Government's Role in the Market — Mitigating the External Effects of Markets
assessment_items.question_text: The chapter notes that Kauṭilya's Arthaśhāstra instructed traders of clarified butter to give buyers a small additional measure to compensate for ghee sticking to the measuring can. What does this historical detail demonstrate?

options.label: A
options.text: It demonstrates that consumer protection — ensuring buyers receive fair quantity and value — is a principle with ancient roots in Indian civilisation, not a recent invention.

options.label: B
options.text: It demonstrates that Indian markets in ancient times traded only in food products such as ghee, unlike the variety found at Hampi.

options.label: C
options.text: It demonstrates that the Arthaśhāstra was a traders' manual focused only on food products and their measurement.

options.label: D
options.text: It demonstrates that the government of ancient India controlled all prices in the market, including the price of clarified butter.

what_each_option_reveals.C: Student reads the specific ghee example as the Arthaśhāstra's entire subject matter, failing to interpret it as a representative illustration of a broader regulatory principle.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Student conflates the chapter's account of ancient consumer-protection instructions with comprehensive price control, over-extending the Arthaśhāstra's role from the single example given.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Student treats the ghee example as evidence of ancient market limitations, ignoring the chapter's Hampi account of a wide range of goods — a cross-section confusion between two different historical examples.
